name: Knee Cartilage Damage (Chondral Defects)
seo_title: Knee Cartilage Damage Palm Beach Gardens | ELITE Sports
seo_desc: Knee cartilage damage care in Palm Beach Gardens and Port St. Lucie, from rehab and injections to MACI restoration, with board-certified Dr. Matarazzo.
lede: A damaged patch in the smooth cartilage lining your knee can cause aching and swelling with activity. Options run from rehab and injections to cartilage restoration surgery.
what_it_is: Articular cartilage is the smooth, white tissue that covers the ends of the bones inside your knee so they glide with very little friction. Cleveland Clinic points out that this cartilage has no direct blood supply, so it usually takes longer to heal than other tissues. Mayo Clinic describes a focal defect as a pothole in otherwise normal cartilage. Even a small one can change how load passes through the joint and may lead to arthritis over time.

Focal cartilage injuries are different from the widespread thinning of osteoarthritis. They usually involve one area and often follow a knee injury. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) notes that cartilage damage is often found while a doctor is treating a related injury, such as a meniscus or ligament tear. According to the AAOS, the best candidates for restoration procedures are usually young adults with a single injury.
symptoms: Knee pain during or after activity, especially weight-bearing
Swelling that comes and goes, often after exercise
Stiffness or difficulty moving the knee smoothly
Catching, clicking or grinding as the knee bends
Pain with stairs, squatting or jumping
causes: A direct blow or fall onto the knee
Meniscus or ACL tears that change how the joint is loaded
A kneecap dislocation that chips the joint surface

how_therapy_helps.intro: Because cartilage repairs itself poorly, treatment aims to calm symptoms and protect the joint. Mayo Clinic notes that physical therapy and injections can reduce symptoms and may slow progression, but they do not replace lost cartilage. When a defect keeps causing pain in an otherwise healthy knee, the AAOS describes several restoration procedures. Dr. Matarazzo considers the size and location of the defect, your age, weight, leg alignment and activity goals, and whether other injuries need treatment at the same time.
methods: Strengthening the thigh and hip muscles and refining movement can reduce load on the damaged area and ease symptoms during daily activity.

Viscosupplement injections may calm pain and swelling. Mayo Clinic cautions that corticosteroid injections can interfere with the knee's ability to form repair tissue, so they are generally not advised for cartilage defects.
Some patients consider platelet-rich plasma or bone marrow concentrate injections. Evidence is still developing, and these injections do not regrow cartilage.
Small holes are made in the bone beneath the defect so a repair tissue can form. The AAOS notes this fibrocartilage is less durable and works best for small lesions.
A plug of healthy cartilage and bone from a low-load area of your knee, or from a donor for larger defects, is moved into the damaged spot.
A two-stage procedure in which your own cartilage cells are grown on a collagen membrane and implanted. The AAOS describes it for defects larger than 2 centimeters.

first_visit: Dr. Matarazzo will ask about past injuries, earlier knee surgeries and which activities bring on pain or swelling. He checks for fluid in the joint, tenderness, alignment of the leg and the stability of the ligaments and menisci. The AAOS notes that cartilage does not show on X-ray, so X-rays are used to check alignment and look for arthritis. An MRI is usually ordered to see the cartilage surface and the bone beneath it.
recovery: Recovery after cartilage restoration is slower than after many other knee procedures, because new tissue has to mature. The AAOS notes that patients may need crutches for several weeks and physical therapy that can include continuous passive motion, and that a full return to sports takes several months. The size and location of the defect, the procedure used and any combined surgery all change the timeline. Nonsurgical care also takes patience, and symptoms may fluctuate with activity level.
self_care: Choose lower-impact exercise such as cycling or swimming while the knee is irritable.
Ice the knee for up to 15 minutes after activity if it swells.
Keep a healthy weight to limit load on the joint.
Avoid deep squats and jumping until the knee has been evaluated.
see_a_doctor: The knee locks or will not straighten fully
Swelling that returns repeatedly after activity
You cannot put weight on the leg
Fever, redness or warmth around the knee
Symptoms that do not improve after three days of home care

faqs.a: Articular cartilage has very limited ability to heal because it has no direct blood supply. Damaged cartilage generally does not regrow on its own, and injections do not rebuild it. Some surgical procedures can fill a defect with repair tissue or transplanted cartilage. Mayo Clinic notes that nonsurgical treatments can ease symptoms but do not restore normal cartilage.

faqs.q: Can cartilage damage be seen on an X-ray?
faqs.a: No. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons explains that articular cartilage contains no calcium, so it does not show up on an X-ray. X-rays still help by showing joint space, alignment and signs of arthritis. An MRI is the usual way to look at the cartilage surface, and some defects are first found during arthroscopy for another problem.

MACI stands for matrix-induced autologous chondrocyte implantation. In a first, small procedure, a sample of your own cartilage cells is taken. Those cells are grown in a lab on a collagen membrane, which is implanted into the defect during a second surgery. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons describes MACI for larger cartilage defects, generally over 2 centimeters.

faqs.q: Who is a good candidate for cartilage restoration?
faqs.a: According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, most candidates are young adults with a single cartilage injury in an otherwise healthy knee. Older patients and people with many damaged areas or widespread arthritis are less likely to benefit. Leg alignment, body weight, ligament stability and the condition of the meniscus also factor into the decision.

faqs.q: Is a cartilage defect the same as arthritis?
faqs.a: They are related but not the same. A focal cartilage defect is a localized area of damage, often from an injury, in a knee that is otherwise healthy. Osteoarthritis involves more widespread cartilage loss across the joint. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that damaged cartilage can lead to arthritis over time, which is one reason defects are evaluated early.

faqs.q: What is microfracture surgery on the knee?
faqs.a: Microfracture is a marrow stimulation procedure. The surgeon makes small holes in the bone under a cartilage defect, which lets blood and cells form a repair tissue. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that this tissue is fibrocartilage, which is less durable than the original cartilage, so microfracture is usually reserved for small defects in less active patients.

signOrSymptom: catching or grinding in the knee
